lessons.title: Iterating Elements with forEach
lessons.description: Use forEach to run a function on every element in an array — the simplest way to loop through data.

sections.heading: What is forEach?
paragraphs: forEach is a method that calls a function once for each element in an array. It's the simplest way to do something with every item without writing a manual loop.

sections.heading: How it works
paragraphs: You pass a function (called a callback) to forEach. JavaScript calls that function for each element, passing three arguments: the current element, its index, and the original array.
list: forEach(callback) — runs the callback for each element
forEach always returns undefined — it doesn't create a new array

codeExamples.heading: forEach basics
explanation: The callback function runs once for each element in the array.
Each time, the color parameter holds the current element's value.
The order is always left to right (index 0, then 1, then 2).

codeExamples.heading: Using the index parameter
explanation: The second parameter gives you the index of the current element.
This is useful when you need to know the position, not just the value.
You can name the parameters anything — (item, i) is also common.

practice.task: Create an array of 3 numbers. Use forEach to log each number doubled.
practice.note: forEach doesn't return anything — it's for side effects like logging or updating the DOM.

keyTakeaways: forEach runs a callback on every element — it's the simplest way to iterate an array.
The callback receives the element, its index, and the original array.
forEach returns undefined — it doesn't create a new array like map does.
lessons.challenge: Given let names = ["Alex", "Sam", "Jordan"], use forEach to log a greeting for each person, like "Hello, Alex!".

lessons.title: Transforming Datasets with map
lessons.description: Create a new array by transforming every element — map doesn't modify the original, it builds a fresh one.

sections.heading: What does map do?
paragraphs: map creates a new array by calling a function on every element of the original. The function's return value becomes the new element at the same position. The original array stays unchanged.

sections.heading: Why map is better than a for loop
paragraphs: Instead of pushing to a new array manually, map handles the creation for you. It's shorter, clearer, and less error-prone. Think of it as "transform each element" rather than "loop and build."

codeExamples.heading: map transforms values
explanation: The callback returns num * 2 for each element, building a new array.
The original numbers array is never modified.
The new array always has the same length as the original.

codeExamples.heading: map with arrow functions
explanation: Arrow functions make map calls concise and readable.
name[0].toUpperCase() capitalizes the first letter, and name.slice(1) keeps the rest.
This is a common pattern: extracting or transforming specific parts of each element.

practice.task: Use map to convert an array of temperatures in Celsius to Fahrenheit. Formula: F = C * 9/5 + 32.
hints: Store the result in a new variable and log it.
practice.note: map always returns a new array of the same length — it never skips elements or changes the original.

keyTakeaways: map creates a new array by transforming each element with a callback function.
The original array is not modified — map is non-destructive.
The new array always has the same length as the original.
lessons.challenge: Given let prices = [10, 20, 50], use map to add 10% tax to each price. Then use map again on the result to round each value to 2 decimal places using .toFixed(2).

lessons.title: Filtering Data with filter
lessons.description: Keep only the elements that pass a test — filter builds a new array with a subset of the original data.

sections.heading: What does filter do?
paragraphs: filter creates a new array containing only the elements that return true from a test function (callback). If the callback returns false, that element is excluded from the new array.

sections.heading: filter vs forEach
paragraphs: forEach runs code on each element but doesn't return anything useful. filter checks each element and builds a new array from the ones that pass. Use filter when you want to keep a subset of data.

codeExamples.heading: filter keeps matching elements
explanation: The callback returns true for even numbers and false for odd ones.
Only elements where the callback returned true end up in the new array.
The original array stays the same — filter is non-destructive.

codeExamples.heading: filter with objects
explanation: Filter works great with arrays of objects — just access the property in the callback.
Only users where age >= 18 is true are included in the result.
This is a common real-world pattern for searching and sorting data.

practice.task: Given let words = ["hi", "hello", "hey", "goodbye"], use filter to create a new array containing only words longer than 3 characters.
hints: The callback checks each word's .length property.
Store the result and log it — you should get ["hello", "goodbye"].
practice.note: filter can return an empty array [] if nothing matches — that's normal, not an error.

keyTakeaways: filter creates a new array with only the elements that pass a test (callback returns true).
The original array is not modified — filter is non-destructive.
The result array can be shorter than the original, or even empty if nothing matches.
lessons.challenge: Given let scores = [85, 42, 91, 67, 55, 73], use filter to get only passing scores (60+). Then count how many passed using .length.

lessons.title: Accumulating Values with reduce
lessons.description: Boil an array down to a single value — reduce processes each element and builds up a result step by step.

sections.heading: What does reduce do?
paragraphs: reduce processes every element in an array and accumulates a single result. It runs a callback that combines the current element with a running total (called the accumulator).

sections.heading: The two required arguments
list: accumulator — the running total (starts at the initial value)
You also get index and array as optional 3rd and 4th arguments
The initial value (second argument to reduce) is important — always provide it

codeExamples.heading: Summing numbers
explanation: The initial value is 0 — this is the starting point for the accumulator.
Each callback return becomes the new acc for the next iteration.

codeExamples.heading: Building an object with reduce
explanation: The initial value is {} — an empty object that we build up.
For each fruit, we either increment its count or start it at 1.
(acc[fruit] || 0) + 1 handles both existing and new entries cleanly.

practice.task: Use reduce to find the largest number in [5, 12, 3, 18, 7]. Hint: start with the first element as the initial value.
hints: Initial value should be the first element: nums[0]
Callback: if (current > acc) return current; return acc;
Or shorter: return current > acc ? current : acc
practice.note: reduce is the most versatile array method — you can implement map, filter, and forEach with it!

keyTakeaways: reduce accumulates all array elements into a single value using a callback.
The accumulator carries the running total — each callback return becomes the next accumulator.
Always provide an initial value (second argument) to avoid unexpected errors.
lessons.challenge: Use reduce to flatten [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6]] into [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. Hint: spread each sub-array into the accumulator.

lessons.title: Searching Arrays: find, findIndex, includes, some, every
lessons.description: Five powerful methods to search arrays — each answers a different question about your data.

sections.heading: The five search methods
paragraphs: JavaScript gives you five ways to search arrays, each suited to a different task:
list: findIndex — returns the index of the first match (or -1)
includes — returns true if the array contains the value
some — returns true if at least one element passes a test
every — returns true if all elements pass a test

codeExamples.heading: find and findIndex
explanation: find returns the first matching object — the whole element, not just the name.
findIndex returns the position (index) where the match was found.
Both stop searching after the first match — they don't check the rest.

codeExamples.heading: includes, some, and every
explanation: includes checks for an exact value match — simple and readable.
some is like an "OR" check — true if any element satisfies the condition.
every is like an "AND" check — true only if all elements satisfy it.

practice.task: Given let products = [{name: "Shirt", price: 25}, {name: "Pants", price: 40}, {name: "Hat", price: 15}], use find to get the first product over $30, and use some to check if any product costs less than $20.
hints: Remember: find returns the element; some returns true/false.
practice.note: find returns undefined and findIndex returns -1 when no match is found — always check for these!

keyTakeaways: find returns the first matching element; findIndex returns its index.
includes checks if a value exists in the array.
some checks if any element passes a test; every checks if all do.
lessons.challenge: Given an array of student objects with name and grade properties, use find to get the first student with grade A, some to check if anyone failed (below 60), and every to verify all students have a name.

lessons.title: Sorting Arrays with Custom Comparators (sort, toSorted)
lessons.description: Put array elements in order — sort modifies the original while toSorted (ES2023) creates a new sorted array.

sections.heading: How sort works
paragraphs: sort() rearranges elements in place. By default, it converts elements to strings and sorts them alphabetically — which is wrong for numbers. You provide a comparator function to control the order.

sections.heading: The comparator function
list: Return 0 if they should stay in the same order

sections.heading: sort vs toSorted
list: sort() — modifies the original array in place, returns the sorted array
toSorted() (ES2023) — returns a new sorted array, leaves original untouched
Use toSorted() when you want to keep the original safe

codeExamples.heading: Sorting numbers correctly
explanation: Without a comparator, [40, 1, 5, 200, 10] sorts as strings: "1", "10", "200", "40", "5".
a - b sorts ascending (smallest first). b - a would sort descending.
The comparator is called multiple times — it should be pure and fast.

codeExamples.heading: toSorted — non-destructive sorting
explanation: toSorted() creates a brand new array — the original stays exactly as it was.
This is the safer choice when you don't want to accidentally change your source data.
Available in modern browsers (2023+). Use [...arr].sort() as a fallback.

practice.task: Sort this array of objects by price (lowest to highest): let items = [{name: "A", price: 30}, {name: "B", price: 10}, {name: "C", price: 20}].
hints: The comparator receives two objects — access the property you want to sort by.
For descending order: (a, b) => b.price - a.price
practice.note: sort is one of the few array methods that modifies the original — use toSorted or [...arr].sort() to keep it safe.

keyTakeaways: Default sort() treats elements as strings — always use a comparator for numbers.
A comparator (a, b) => a - b sorts ascending; b - a sorts descending.
toSorted() (ES2023) returns a new array without modifying the original.
Both sort and toSorted can sort objects by any property using a custom comparator.
lessons.challenge: Sort this array of students by grade (highest first), then alphabetically by name for ties: [{name: "Zoe", grade: 85}, {name: "Alex", grade: 92}, {name: "Sam", grade: 92}]. The result should be Alex, Sam, Zoe.
